scenes.text: So, which supplements actually work? Four products sit on a shelf: a protein powder, a caffeine tablet, a creatine powder, and a multivitamin. All four are legal and marketed to athletes. Rank them from most to least likely to improve a seventeen-year-old team-sport athlete's performance. Then the question that matters more: for your top choice, what would have to be true about the athlete for it to help?

Start with food first. Most needs are met by ordinary food, timed well. A supplement is something added on top, and it earns its place only for a reason. There are three. A diagnosed deficiency, like low iron found by a blood test, that food alone is correcting too slowly. A practical problem, like a recovery drink between two matches on one day, when there's no time or appetite for food. Or a specific ergogenic effect, meaning performance-boosting, at a dose ordinary food can't deliver, which is where caffeine and creatine come in. Notice what isn't on the list. "Everyone else takes it." "The tub says it helps recovery." And "just in case my diet has gaps", which is insurance against a problem nobody has checked for. So ask two questions. What problem does it solve? And does this athlete have that problem?

Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals. They supply no energy, but the systems that do can't work without them. Iron is part of haemoglobin, so it carries oxygen, and adolescent female athletes and endurance athletes are most at risk of running low. Here's the key idea. Correcting a deficiency, a real shortfall, improves performance. Adding more to an athlete who isn't deficient doesn't, and too much iron is harmful. So iron should follow a blood test, not a guess. Protein works the same way. As you've seen, training is the stimulus, and protein the material. Once intake is adequate, more protein doesn't build more muscle. A powder can help when food can't practically reach that adequate amount, but then it's convenience, not magic.

Caffeine and creatine have the strongest evidence. Caffeine acts on the brain. It lowers how hard effort feels and sharpens alertness and reaction time. The work still costs the same, it just feels easier. It helps endurance, repeated sprints and concentration. But it can cause anxiety, a racing heart, an upset stomach, and, taken late, poor sleep, which damages recovery, so it can't replace sleep. Teenagers are generally advised to limit it. Creatine works in the muscle. In Year 11 you met phosphocreatine, the fuel that rebuilds ATP in the first few seconds of a sprint. Creatine enlarges that store, so more maximal work is done before it runs low, and it refills faster between efforts. That suits repeated sprints and strength training. It doesn't help long endurance, where glycogen is the limit, and it adds body mass, mostly water.

Now the other side, because discuss means weighing. First, contamination. A product can contain something not on its label, from a shared factory line or deliberately added. In sport, the athlete is responsible for whatever is in their body, so "it was in my supplement" isn't a defence. That's how athletes fail drug tests without meaning to. Independently batch-tested products reduce the risk, but don't remove it. Second, side effects and interactions with medication. Third, cost, and the bigger cost: attention taken away from sleep, food and training, which matter far more. And a teammate swearing by it is weak evidence, because believing in a product can itself improve performance, the placebo effect.

So a discuss answer judges each one on the same points: the claim, how it works, the evidence, the limits, and who it actually suits. Caffeine: strong evidence, for athletes who've trialled it and aren't covering for poor sleep. Creatine: strong evidence for repeated sprints and strength, where extra mass isn't a penalty. Micronutrients: clear benefit only when correcting a tested deficiency. Protein powder: useful only when food can't reach an adequate intake. So, the hook. Our athlete is seventeen, and under eighteen, supplements generally aren't recommended: food first, and performance supplements only on medical or dietitian advice. For adults, caffeine and creatine probably rank above protein powder and a multivitamin. And for every one, it depends on the athlete. Does a test show a deficiency? Is sleep sorted? Does the sport reward short, repeated power?
Two things to remember. Ask what problem it solves, and whether the athlete has it. And correct a lack, but don't add more.

Two exam questions. First. A sixteen-year-old vegetarian rower has never had a blood test, but wants an iron supplement because a teammate takes one. A fifteen-year-old trains straight after school, then rides a bus for an hour, can't eat a meal until eight, and asks about a protein drink. Discuss supplement use for each. Pause here to answer.

The rower has no diagnosed deficiency, only a guess, and too much iron is harmful. So test first, and eat iron-rich foods. The fifteen-year-old has a real practical problem, so a recovery drink after training, even flavoured milk, can be justified as convenience, then food at home. The classic mistake is treating both as the same decision.

Second. A seventeen-year-old swimmer plans to take a caffeine tablet for the first time before an evening state final, using a product bought online with an incomplete ingredient list. Evaluate this plan. Pause here to answer.

Caffeine has strong evidence, but a first try on final night risks anxiety, a racing heart and lost sleep. An incomplete label is a contamination risk the swimmer is responsible for. A poor plan. At seventeen, food first: no caffeine tablet unless a doctor or sports dietitian advises it, then trialled in training with a batch-tested product. The classic mistake is judging only whether caffeine works.

So start with food, ask what problem a supplement solves and whether the athlete has it, and weigh the evidence against risks the label won't show. Creatine works by filling the phosphocreatine store. But having energy available is half the story. The other half is using it well. How does biomechanics make movement more efficient?
